o: We need employees whose three most recent reviews (by date) have strictly increasing ratings, plus the improvement score (latest minus earliest of those three). Employees with fewer than three reviews are excluded. Window functions make this natural: rank each employee's reviews from most recent, keep ranks 1–3, then verify strict increase with LAG and compute the score with MAX−MIN.
k: ROW_NUMBER over review_date DESC isolates the last three reviews per employee.
LAG lets us compare each rating with the previous one to enforce strict increase.
COUNT(*) = 3 in HAVING enforces the minimum-review requirement.

a.i: Rank reviews newest-first per employee, discard anything past rank 3, then within that trio require each rating to exceed the previous one. The improvement score is simply MAX(rating) − MIN(rating) over the trio, since strict increase makes the latest the max and the earliest the min.
s: CTE 1: ROW_NUMBER() PARTITION BY employee_id ORDER BY review_date DESC.
Keep rows with rn <= 3; add LAG(rating) ordered by rn.
Join to employees; GROUP BY employee; HAVING COUNT(*)=3 and every row strictly greater than its predecessor.
Output score = MAX(rating) − MIN(rating), ordered by score DESC then name ASC.

c.python:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT employee_id, rating,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY employee_id ORDER BY review_date DESC) AS rn
  FROM performance_reviews
),
lagged AS (
  SELECT employee_id, rating,
         LAG(rating) OVER (PARTITION BY employee_id ORDER BY rn) AS prev_r
  FROM ranked
  WHERE rn <= 3
)
SELECT e.employee_id, e.name,
       MAX(l.rating) - MIN(l.rating) AS improvement_score
FROM lagged l
JOIN employees e ON e.employee_id = l.employee_id
GROUP BY e.employee_id, e.name
HAVING COUNT(*) = 3
   AND SUM(CASE WHEN l.prev_r IS NULL OR l.rating > l.prev_r THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) = 3
ORDER BY improvement_score DESC, name ASC;

a.t: O(R log R) — sorting/window ordering over all reviews R
a.sp: O(R) for the windowed intermediate rows

w: Window functions are the idiomatic tool here; a correlated-subquery alternative (fetching the 1st/2nd/3rd newest rating separately) works but is slower and messier. Pitfall: forgetting that ties in review_date need a deterministic tiebreaker (add review_id to the ORDER BY if dates can repeat), and using >= instead of > which would admit flat trajectories like David Wilson's.
